title: Received tradition
hookLine: Kabbalah means "receiving", the name for Jewish mystical tradition

cards: Buy a coffee in Tel Aviv and ask for a receipt, and the Hebrew word you'll hear is kabbalah.
The same word names something that sounds nothing like a coffee shop: the Jewish mystical tradition, with its talk of God's hidden life and the secret depths of the Torah.
One word for a slip of paper and a doorway into mystery. And it says something about where this tradition thinks its wisdom comes from.

teach.h: A ROOT THAT MEANS TO RECEIVE.
teach.b: Kabbalah. First, the root. Kabbalah comes from a Hebrew root meaning to receive.

A receipt is what you receive. It's the same root in the opening line of Pirkei Avot: Moses received the Torah from Sinai and handed it on to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, and onward, teacher to student.
Kabbalah, at its simplest, is what has been received. Second, receiving in daily life.
On Friday evening, synagogues pray a service called Kabbalat Shabbat, receiving the Sabbath, welcoming it in like a guest at the door.
So the word lives in ordinary Jewish life before it ever means mysticism. Third, the name for a tradition.

Over time, Kabbalah became the name for a body of Jewish mystical teaching: how God, who is beyond all knowing, is still revealed in the world, and the hidden layers of meaning in the letters of the Torah.
You met a hint of it when the Ramban spoke of meanings known by the way of truth. Among its books is the Zohar, the radiance, which this block will come to.
Fourth, received, not invented. The mystics didn't call their teaching discovery or innovation. They called it what was received, something handed down.
Whatever a reader concludes about its history, the name says how its teachers understood themselves: as links in a chain.
And they read old texts closely, like Isaiah's vision of the seraphim calling out, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts."

how: Jews welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening with the Kabbalat Shabbat service, and those who study Kabbalah read its texts, such as the Zohar, often in study groups or with a teacher.

games.q: you're naming a tradition of hidden teaching about God and the Torah. what name do the Jewish mystics choose?
o: a word meaning the new light.
games.why: Kabbalah: the received. the name says its teachers saw themselves as links in a chain, not inventors.

practice: Say one line from Isaiah's vision, a text Jewish mystics read closely, once and slowly, out loud or silently: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts." Don't try to decode it; just notice which word stays with you, and let it echo.
If you don't pray, receive it simply as an old line handed down for a very long time, the way you'd receive a gift.

wordCard.voice: Kabbalah. From a Hebrew root meaning to receive: a receipt, the welcoming of Shabbat, and the name of the Jewish mystical tradition. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: receiving, what is received; also a receipt, and the name of Jewish mystical tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: the received. The word for mystery starts as a word for receiving. A new road starts here.
